analysis.one_liner: Orders a government study of grocery price increases and ideas to lower them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which only ordered a government study of grocery costs, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Government Accountability Office — Congress's nonpartisan investigative arm — to study how much food-at-home prices rose over 20 years and to recommend ways to bring grocery costs down for consumers. It did not itself change any prices or set any rules; it only commissioned a report, due 180 days after enactment, for three congressional committees. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to a committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary shoppers would have been the intended beneficiaries of a government report documenting grocery price increases and recommending policy responses. No company or industry gains directly, though the study's recommendations could have been the first step toward future legislation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the Comptroller General to study changes in the Consumer Price Index for food at home over the 20 years ending at enactment, plus other economic metrics needed to assess the impact of food-at-home costs on U.S. consumers [S2].
It required a written report to Congress within 180 days containing the study's findings and recommendations to help lower food-at-home costs for U.S. consumers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have been limited to the modest expense of a GAO study. Because the bill contained no mandates, taxes, or regulations, no business or household would have borne a direct cost — though any future legislation built on its recommendations could have.
analysis.who_pays_short: No one, beyond the study's cost

drawbacks.text: The bill commissioned a study rather than taking any direct action, so it would not have lowered a single grocery price on its own; its value depended entirely on whether Congress later acted on the recommendations [S2].

A 20-year price study arriving after the worst grocery inflation in decades risks documenting a problem consumers already live with, and the bill gave no deadline for Congress to respond to the report [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost was trivial and the potential benefit real but indirect: a credible, nonpartisan record of how grocery prices moved over two decades, with policy recommendations. It was a first-step bill, and its weakness was that it committed Congress to nothing beyond producing a report.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcus Molinaro introduced the bill on June 28, 2024, with Reps. Ryan, Ciscomani, and Davis of North Carolina as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S2][S4].
The bill attracted five cosponsors in total — four House Democrats and one House Republican [S3].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete, since the bill only commissioned a study. The status quo continued unchanged: grocery prices stayed where they were, and no government report examining them was ever produced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no study was done

for.name: Rep. Marcus J. Molinaro
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on June 28, 2024.

for.name: 1 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (beyond the sponsor and original cosponsors).

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 28, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican sponsor, original cosponsors from both parties, and five cosponsors split 4 Democrats to 1 Republican — and no one opposed it on the record; it simply never advanced [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill as introduced imposed nothing on the food industry — it only ordered a study. But its purpose was to document food price increases and recommend ways to lower them, so had it advanced, the industry could have faced scrutiny or future policy proposals aimed at its pricing. The industry's interest in avoiding such scrutiny runs against consumers who pay the prices.
